subject: Computer Networking
title: NotPetya: The Costliest Cyberattack
description: One-minute skill: NotPetya: The Costliest Cyberattack.

hook.text: NotPetya looked like ransomware. But it had no decryption. Its only purpose was destruction.

buildup.text: It spread via a Ukrainian accounting software update. Within hours it escaped Ukraine and hit global firms.

discovery.text: Maersk, FedEx, Merck, and Mondelez were devastated. Maersk lost nearly all of its IT systems.

twist.text: Maersk rebuilt 45,000 PCs and 4,000 servers in ten days. A heroic recovery effort under extreme pressure.

climax.text: Total global damage exceeded $10 billion. It remains the costliest cyberattack in history.

punchline.text: NotPetya wasn't ransomware. It was a weapon disguised as one.

quiz.question: How did NotPetya initially spread?
options: Through a compromised Ukrainian accounting software update
Via phishing emails to individual employees
Through infected USB drives distributed at a conference

details.summary: NotPetya was a Russian cyberweapon disguised as ransomware that spread through a Ukrainian tax software update in June 2017. It caused over ten billion dollars in damage worldwide, crippling Maersk, Merck, FedEx, and countless other companies. It remains the costliest cyberattack in history.
details.whyItMatters: NotPetya proved that cyberweapons cannot be contained. A targeted attack on Ukraine cascaded through supply chains to devastate companies worldwide that had no connection to the original target.
takeaways: NotPetya caused over ten billion dollars in global damage
It spread through a legitimate software update mechanism
Supply chain attacks can cascade far beyond intended targets

faq.question: How did NotPetya spread so far beyond Ukraine?
faq.answer: It initially spread through the M.E.Doc tax software update used by Ukrainian businesses. But multinational companies with Ukrainian offices got infected and the worm spread through their internal networks globally. Maersk lost nearly every server across 600 sites in 45 countries.

faq.question: Why is NotPetya considered a cyberweapon and not ransomware?
faq.answer: Although it displayed a ransom demand, the encryption was irreversible. There was no mechanism to decrypt files even if paid. It was designed to destroy data, not collect money. Security researchers attributed it to Russian military intelligence targeting Ukraine.
